Question: The area of the largest triangle that can be inscribed in a semicircle whose radius is \(r\) is:
Solution:
Place the semicircle with its diameter horizontal. For radius \(r>0\), it fits in a rectangle of width \(2r\) and height \(r\). We can use these dimensions to bound any inscribed triangle, without assuming that one side is the diameter.

For a nondegenerate triangle, call its lowest vertex \(P\), its highest vertex \(Q\), and its remaining vertex \(T\), breaking height ties arbitrarily. The horizontal line through \(T\) meets the opposite side \(PQ\) at a point \(S\). The segment \(TS\) splits the triangle into two triangles with the same horizontal base \(TS\).

Write \(b=TS\), and let \(h_1,h_2\) be the perpendicular heights of \(P,Q\) above or below that horizontal line. Both endpoints of \(TS\) lie in the rectangle, so \(b\le 2r\). Also, \(h_1+h_2\) is the vertical separation of the lowest and highest vertices, so \(h_1+h_2\le r\). Therefore the area \(K\) satisfies
\[
K=\frac12bh_1+\frac12bh_2
=\frac12b(h_1+h_2)
\le\frac12(2r)r=r^2.
\]
This also covers a height tie, when one smaller triangle has area zero. A degenerate triangle has area zero as well.

Finally, choose the diameter endpoints and the point on the arc directly above the center. Their triangle has base \(2r\) and height \(r\), so its area is \(r^2\). Thus the largest area is \(\boxed{r^2}\), choice A.
